source.title: Copying Before Suppression: What Drives a Below-Chance Dip During Language Model Training?

page_placements.theme: Training changes IOI mechanisms and their causal signs

record.tranche_reason: The study uses causal interventions and behavioural evaluations on IOI across training, but does not reproduce the original GPT-2 Small circuit-finding procedure or evaluate its 26-head, seven-class circuit.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many IOI interventions and behavioural results. Values used only to select heads or layer bands are not recorded as outcomes. Findings on Greater-Than, factual recall, subject-verb agreement, and the symbolic task are not rows because they do not measure the IOI behaviour named in these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study's own results bear on V3 in a new setting: training dynamics across Pythia sizes and two independently trained GPT-2 Small runs. It selects a mature head that suppresses the repeated name and shows it contributes substantially at maturity but is nearly inert at early checkpoints. It bears weakly on V6 through second-mention (S2) state patching at maturity on hand-written varied-syntax prompts. It never reconstructs or evaluates the 26-head, seven-class circuit, so V1, V2, V4 and V5 are untested. Most rows measure a different construct: the below-chance early-training window and causal reversals at the block or residual-state level.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the below-chance IOI window reflects a temporary imbalance. Repeated-name copying heads are already causally harmful at the floor, while a later-developing suppressing head is nearly inert, and LM loss masks this. The detailed copying-to-suppression account holds for Pythia 160M, 410M and 1B. Other Pythia sizes, GPT-2 and OLMo show related early-to-late reversals, not one shared circuit.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates IOI during training using causal activation replacements, head-output replacements, and parameter transplants. It does not apply the original GPT-2 Small circuit-finding and faithfulness/completeness/minimality evaluation recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured effects differ by training checkpoint and intervention site. At Pythia 160M the S2 replacement effect changes sign from floor to maturity; its magnitude varies across layer bands. Matched and norm-matched random S2 replacements are close. The three-name margin intervals are less consistently positive than the IO-minus-S measure. Naturalised prompts and multi-token-name prompts change the evaluation setting; the latter is behavioural only.

fits_no_version.finding: IOI accuracy falls below chance early in training while LM loss decreases. At the floor, a frozen ensemble of heads that copy the repeated name causally favours S.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early in training, models pass through a below-chance IOI window driven by harmful repeated-name copying heads before suppression develops.

fits_no_version.finding: The causal role of the S2 residual state reverses sign between floor and maturity. This holds in Pythia 160M–12B, in OLMo-1B and on varied syntax, and matched and random replacement agree.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The S2-position state is harmful early and necessary later; the reversal recurs across scales and model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Repetition-sensitive state at the first feed-forward block and at the input is harmful at the floor. It reverses to helpful at maturity in Pythia 2.8B and in the GPT-2 CRFM runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-layer repetition-sensitive computation switches from harmful to helpful for IOI over training.

fits_no_version.finding: Transplanting the mature suppressor's parameters into the floor checkpoint closes 35–68% of the floor-to-mature LD gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single later-learned suppression head is partially sufficient to rescue early IOI behaviour.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper limits its strongest head-level causal account to three primary Pythia sizes. Several cross-model extensions use different interventions and do not establish a common circuit. The 1B Pythia trajectory has sparse checkpoints. The control-mean head experiment has only three or four top-level template groups; the authors report nested and item-clustered intervals. Multi-token-name and some prompt-variant results are behavioural only, without causal circuit tests.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant IOI results omitted under the 60-row limit. Other-task experiments were left out because they do not measure the IOI behaviour specified by these versions.

untested.parts: All of it. The GPT-2 Small 26-head, seven-class circuit and its faithfulness, completeness and minimality are never evaluated.
All of it. No name-mover ablation or backup-head self-repair test.

Only a single suppressing head is identified per model. There is no full head-class decomposition (duplicate-token, S-inhibition, name-mover). The larger Pythia sizes and OLMo get no head-level analysis. Component reuse on other tasks is not tested: the factual-recall head is task-specific.
All of it. Circuit-finding methods and ablation types are not compared for recovering the same circuit.
All of it. The IOI circuit's faithfulness and completeness are never computed under alternative ablations, metrics or prompt distributions.
Component-level circuit identity across templates. Name-order results reported separately. Prompts with more than two names. Any mechanism for multi-token names.

missing.what: Mature suppressor characterisation: END→S2 attention 0.934/0.336/0.527 and direct S projection −6.22/−2.10/−7.27. Backward trace to floor: attention 0.009/0.062/0.014, projection −0.034/−0.005/−0.025.
Cumulative reconstruction at 410M: the suppressor plus 8 correct-name-writing heads closes 88.1% of the gap (accuracy 0.933). This indicates a suppressor/name-writer division of labour.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked most rows to V5, but no row evaluates the IOI circuit's faithfulness or completeness. They concern the study's own early-training interventions, so V5 is untested. Stage errors: R39 and R43 are step-1500 checkpoints, not mature. R14 and R15 give step 2000, but the separately trained 160M floor is step 2850. For V6, the mature S2 rows are 'observed' relative to the version, not 'reversed'. The V3 support is limited to a single suppressing role. The authors note the suppressor head identity differs between GPT-2 runs.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the GPT-2 Small 26-head, seven-class circuit, its faithfulness, completeness, or minimality, or the claim that removing everything outside that circuit preserves IOI.
The study does not ablate the main name-mover heads to test self-repair or backup heads taking over their role.

The study tests IOI-related causal effects in other models and training checkpoints, but does not establish that the same head classes and roles recur across them. It does not test reuse of the IOI components for other tasks.
The study does not compare circuit-finding methods, ablation types, and metrics to determine whether they recover essentially the same circuit.
The study compares some interventions, outcome measures, and prompt sets, but does not estimate faithfulness or completeness of the original 26-head circuit under those alternatives.

The study evaluates varied templates, names, and multi-token answers behaviourally, and tests second-mention state replacement on varied syntax. It does not test the full copying-head circuit on these prompt variants or test prompts with more than two candidate names.
